newsitem.title: BRAZIL: COCOA--Brazil prices shoot up, reason unclear.
newsitem.headline: COCOA--Brazil prices shoot up, reason unclear.

text.p: Cocoa prices in Brazil shot up this week but dealers said it was unclear how much the increase was due to the abolition of a sales tax and how much it was due to a battle between grinders and shippers.
Cocoa beans were fetching between 15 and 16 Real per 15-kilo arroba at the start of last week but on Thursday the price paid to farmers had risen to between 18 and 19 Real.
Dealers said that one of the reasons was the abolition last week of the ICMS sales tax which is not longer charged on exported commodities.
Until last week, shippers and grinders had officially been responsible for paying the 13 percent tax but in practice had discounted the amount from the price they paid to farmers.
Although international prices rose in the last week, dealers said that farmers, who until two weeks ago were being paid below the export price, were now being given a premium.
"People at the moment are paying 19 Real when they should be paying 17.5 or 18 Real," said a trader.
Dealers said that the premium was not entirely due to the removal of the ICMS tax and said that grinders were paying over the odds to stop shippers getting hold of the cocoa.
"The industries need the raw material to keep their machines going and they are pushing the market over the FOB values," said a dealer.
Dealers said that industries had also got jumpy after hearing of a shipment of around 60,000 to 70,000 60-kilo bags for export in October-November.
However, dealers said the industries had got the wrong end of the stick and the shipment was merely an August commitment that had been rolled forward by a company.
"They heard about the shipment, got nervous and pushed the price up higher than it should be," the dealer said.

Farmers said plentiful rain had fallen throughout the cocoa region in the last ten days, ending a drought that had lasted nearly three months and reduced the October-April main crop to around 1.0 million 60-kilo bags.
"The damage has been done to the main crop but at least the soil moisture is higher," said Ronaldo Monteiro.

"Cocoa trees are miraculous things. In a few days, they have changed completely. The leaves are much healthier and bulbs for the next crop are appearing. If we have decent rain, I think the midcrop (May-September) will begin early."
